assessment.nobel_worthiness: The BLP demand-estimation framework with random-coefficients discrete choice, plus the Ericson-Pakes dynamic industry framework, turned industrial organisation into a quantitative empirical field. The methods are now standard in merger analysis, antitrust, trade and environmental policy, so the practical and scientific reach is very large.
assessment.attribution: The core demand-system contribution is Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes, with Berry's 1994 inversion as a key step. Pakes also has the dynamic-games and estimation work. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are credited on the longlist but are more clearly adjacent contributors, and the three-name limit keeps the core.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The work dates from 1994-95 and has had three decades of validation and widespread use in applied work.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer to include Bresnahan or Reiss for empirical IO more broadly.
Whether the prize is read as a methods prize or a prize for economic discoveries.
My recollection of the contribution details is not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work builds a systematic theory and empirics of how constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes. It created modern political economics as a field, and the integration of politics into policy analysis is central to the discipline.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the clear pair for the constitutional and electoral-rules programme. Besley is a strong third through state capacity and political agency. The credit is concentrated and coherent.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with major work from the 1990s to the 2000s and a large literature built on it. The 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity overlaps in theme but not in the core contribution.
uncertainties: Overlap with the recent prize on institutions could count against timing.
Persson's long Stockholm affiliation could raise conflict-of-interest considerations, to be disclosed, not adjudicated.
Causal identification of the empirical constitutional results is debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based framework for technology and the 'China shock' evidence changed how economists understand labour-demand shifts, polarisation, wage inequality and the local costs of trade. The work has strong empirical credibility and clear policy relevance.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the central figure on both task-based technology and trade shocks. Hanson and Dorn are co-authors on the China shock. The task framework also draws on Acemoglu and Restrepo and on Katz-Murphy, who are not in this credited set apart from Katz.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature. The China-shock work is from 2013-16 and the task approach from 2003. Some of the long-run conclusions are still being debated.
uncertainties: Overlap with prior prizes on technology and growth and on labour-market empirics.
Robustness and interpretation of the China-shock estimates are still contested.
The longlist omits some who developed the task framework.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki-Moore credit cycles showed how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. With the financial-accelerator line, this became the main framework for macro-financial linkages, which proved central after 2008 and is widely used in policy models.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore are the core pair for the collateral-constraint mechanism. Gertler's financial-accelerator and later work with Kiyotaki is the natural third. Bernanke, who shared the 2022 prize, overlaps through the accelerator, so the credit is entangled with that earlier award.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The work dates from 1997, with extensive follow-up and empirical use.
uncertainties: The 2022 prize for banks and financial crises may be read as having covered part of this territory.
The question of whether Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist should be treated differently from Kiyotaki-Moore.
Fit of the models to the data is imperfect.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities, the Calvo pricing model, policy rules and the microfounded New Keynesian framework underlie modern central-bank analysis. The impact on both the theory and practice of monetary policy is enormous.
assessment.attribution: Credit is widely diffused across Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and others. Any three-person selection is contestable, so the ballot is harder to defend on attribution than on importance.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with decades of use and refinement. The framework has also been tested by the post-2008 and post-2021 inflation experiences.
uncertainties: The three-person limit forces an arbitrary exclusion of major contributors.
The framework's performance and critiques after the inflation surge.
Overlap with earlier prizes on rational expectations and monetary policy.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation research programme quantified how distortions across firms can explain a large share of cross-country income differences. It reshaped development accounting and productivity analysis and linked micro data to macro outcomes.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh-Klenow (2009) is the central paper. Restuccia-Rogerson is a closely related and independent contribution, and Restuccia is credited here, so attribution is plausibly shared. Two names are proposed to keep the core of the contribution.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature, as the work dates from 2008-09 and has a large follow-up literature. Some measurement-based critiques are still unsettled.
uncertainties: Sensitivity of estimates to measurement error and to the model's assumptions.
Whether Restuccia and Rogerson deserve equal credit.
Whether the committee sees the work as a method more than a discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Alternating-offers bargaining gives a tractable non-cooperative foundation for bargaining outcomes. It links to the Nash solution and to decentralised-market bargaining, and the framework underpins work across labour, macro, trade and industrial organisation.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is the central contribution. Rubinstein-Wolinsky covers bargaining in markets. Binmore has related work and Stahl is a precursor, but the credit most naturally goes to the first two.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with four decades of influence. The long gap may mean the committee has judged it before.
uncertainties: Game theory has been recognised several times, which may reduce the field's priority.
Whether the committee sees this as foundational enough compared with applied empirical candidates.
Binmore's role relative to Wolinsky.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data gave new evidence on intergenerational mobility, neighbourhood effects and the causal importance of place. The work has both scientific and public-policy impact and set new empirical standards.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is clearly central. Hendren and Friedman are major collaborators, especially on the Opportunity Atlas and the neighbourhood-effects research. Katz's earlier Moving to Opportunity work is also related, so the credit is partly shared.
assessment.maturity: Relatively young, as the main results date from 2014 onwards. Long-term replication and policy outcomes are still being assessed.
uncertainties: The scientific durability of the findings is not fully established.
Possible early timing relative to the careers involved.
Attribution among a large team and across the earlier mobility literature.
